description:
This study asks whether prayer is optional, what it means to pray without ceasing, and why Christians should pray when God is sovereign. Wesam Saad begins by recalling prayer’s purpose as communion with God. He then explains the command to pray continually as an ongoing awareness of God’s presence, dependence on him and submission to his will, rather than abandoning daily responsibilities for uninterrupted spoken prayer.

Connecting prayer with giving thanks in every situation, Saad distinguishes gratitude within hardship from calling the hardship itself good. He also affirms the importance of time set apart for personal communion with God. Continual dependence throughout ordinary activities and focused time alone with the Father belong together. Prayer should express a living relationship, not become a mechanical task that is merely checked off.

The discussion then considers God’s knowledge and decrees. Saad explains that prayer expresses love, obeys God’s command and reshapes the believer’s desires. He adds that God appoints both outcomes and the means through which they occur. Ezekiel’s prophetic obedience and Elijah’s prayers illustrate the privilege of participating in God’s work. The session encourages thankful, persistent prayer grounded in God’s power and personal relationship with his people.

questions.question: Why does Saad say that prayer is not optional for Christians?
questions.answer: He explains “pray without ceasing” as an ongoing command, not merely a description of an unusually devoted person. Prayer is therefore part of the believer’s continuing life before God, rather than a last resort after every other possibility has been exhausted.

questions.question: Does praying without ceasing require Christians to neglect work and family responsibilities?
questions.answer: Saad explicitly rejects that interpretation. He describes a heart continually conscious of God’s presence, dependent on him and submitted to his will while carrying out ordinary responsibilities. The discussion uses breathing as an illustration of something that continues while other activities take place.

questions.question: How does giving thanks relate to continual prayer?
questions.answer: Saad connects the command to pray with the following instruction to give thanks in everything. He distinguishes thanking God within a painful situation from thanking him for the suffering itself. No circumstance removes the believer’s need to remain prayerfully dependent and thankful.

questions.question: Why does he also emphasise time alone with God?
questions.answer: Awareness of God throughout the day does not remove the value of focused personal communion. Saad affirms Jesus’ example of withdrawing to be with the Father and describes how that communion strengthens believers to respond to trials. He warns against turning it into a mechanical exercise.

questions.question: Why speak to God when he already knows what we are going to say?
questions.answer: Saad compares prayer with communicating love or pain within a personal relationship. Knowing the information does not make that communication pointless. Prayer expresses love, trust and communion with the Father; it is deeper than submitting a request and waiting for an output.

questions.question: How can prayer change the person who prays?
questions.answer: Saad explains that prayer can redirect attention from the immediate problem to God’s greatness, wisdom and purposes. Through communion, the believer’s affections and will are realigned with God’s will, rather than remaining centred only on the desired outcome.

questions.question: How does God’s appointing means as well as outcomes encourage prayer?
questions.answer: Saad teaches that God brings about his purposes through means, including prayer. He uses Ezekiel’s obedience and Elijah’s prayers to show the privilege of being involved in what God does. Divine sovereignty therefore does not make prayer useless; it gives believers reason to depend on God and participate in his work.
